name: Gareth Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fenwick Growers, which grows broccoli, leeks and salad for two of the big supermarkets. It's flat, wet land, about four hundred hectares, plus a packhouse where everything gets washed, trimmed and boxed. I'm a field hand, two years in, but because I'm good with phones and tablets I've ended up running the harvest tablet for the broccoli crew, logging what's cut, where, and how many crates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. There are twelve of us in broccoli season, half from abroad, and lunch on the trailer is the best hour of the day, six languages and one flask of terrible coffee. What wears me out is the supermarket. If they ring at six in the morning and want two thousand more heads by noon, the whole day changes and everyone's back aches by three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you're good with tablets. Do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, yes. I use a translation app for the crew, and I ask an AI chat to help me plan the next day's rows when the order changes. I'm not the best on the knife, honestly, the guys from Romania cut twice as fast as me, so the tech is where I'm actually useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, keep it coming, it already helps me every day. I'd probably post a screenshot of it planning a harvest. People at the farm already call me the phone guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my little job on the tablet gets easier and maybe more important. If the AI can talk to the supermarket's order system, I'd be the one setting it up. I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Fenwick if I can try connecting the orders straight into the harvest plan. Maybe do a short online course on farm software in the evenings. Keep saving, we've got about four months put away, me and Dev.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited, like a new toy at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boyfriend, we live together above the bakery on Station Road. He's a junior accountant at a firm in town. He uses more AI than I do and complains about it more, which is funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the crew who wouldn't like this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in this one, no. Most of the crew use translation apps already to text home. Andrei, who's been coming for nine years, says the apps make him sound like a robot, but he still uses them.

S0.say: I'd say keep it coming, because it already helps me every day. I'd post a screenshot of it planning a harvest, since people already call me the phone guy.
S0.think: I think my tablet job gets easier and maybe more important. If the AI could talk to the supermarket's order system, I'd want to be the one setting it up.
S0.do: Asks Mr Fenwick to let him link supermarket orders to the harvest plan. Takes a short evening course in farm software and keeps saving with Dev.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like getting a new toy at work.
S0.quote: If the AI can talk to the supermarket's order system, I'd be the one setting it up. I'd like that.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth's place on the farm comes from tech, not field skill, and he's open about that. His partner is an office worker, which may matter later. He was relaxed and keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for young people, because beginners need a way in. I got in through the back door, as a picker, and worked up a tiny bit. I'd say supermarkets should pay enough that farms can afford to train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's mostly fine for me, maybe good. Slow change means I get time to become the person who understands the new kit. But Dev's firm hiring fewer beginners worries me, he's still junior there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a proper qualification, the agricultural tech certificate at the college, one day a week. I'd ask Fenwick to pay half, and I'd pay the rest from savings. That's maybe six hundred, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Dev, fine for me. I keep looking at it from two sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said supermarkets should pay more. Do you blame them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, mostly. They set the price, they change the order at six in the morning, and they'd buy from abroad if we said no. Fenwick isn't rich, whatever people think, he drives a twelve-year-old car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Dev's firm stopped hiring beginners, what would that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean Dev's stuck as the most junior forever, doing the boring bits nobody else wants. He'd get grumpy and talk about leaving. I'd tell him to stay put until he has something else, because we can't both be stuck at the bottom.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame for young people who need a way in. Supermarkets should pay enough that farms can afford to train beginners.
S1.think: I think slow change is mostly fine or even good for me, because I get time to learn the new kit. What worries me is Dev's firm hiring fewer juniors.
S1.do: Enrols in the agricultural tech certificate at college one day a week. Asks Fenwick to pay half and covers the rest, about six hundred, from savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy for Dev and fine for himself, looking at it from two sides.
S1.quote: Fenwick isn't rich, whatever people think, he drives a twelve-year-old car.
S1.fieldNote: He blames the supermarkets clearly and defends his boss. He sees slow AI as time to build skills, and he's willing to spend his own savings on it. His worry has already started to shift toward his partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for office workers, like money while they retrain, and a say for unions in how AI gets used. Online I'd be posting a lot, probably too much. I'd also say farms need some of those new AI jobs too, not just cities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Dev. Routine office work is exactly what a junior accountant does all day, the checking, the spreadsheets. He's said himself that half his week could be done by a program already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help him look at what else he could do with his skills, maybe the accounting side of farms and growers, because they're always behind with the books. I'd keep our savings for his gap, not mine. I'd also pitch to Fenwick that the farm needs a data person, and that could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Dev. But also, weirdly, a bit hopeful for me, which I don't say out loud to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the night be like when Dev came home with bad news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go quiet and start tidying the kitchen, that's his thing. I'd order pizza and not talk about it until he does. Then probably at midnight he'd want to make a spreadsheet of our money, because of course he would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're hopeful for you. What would the data job actually involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matching what we pick to what the supermarket orders, so we don't cut broccoli that ends up in the bin. Last week we threw away about forty crates because the order dropped after we'd cut. If I can stop that, I've paid for myself.

S2.say: I'd say office workers need money while they retrain and unions need a say in how AI is used. I'd add that farms need some of the new AI jobs, not just cities.
S2.think: Privately it's Dev I worry about, because a junior accountant's routine checking is exactly what's being automated. He's said half his week could already be done by a program.
S2.do: Helps Dev look at bookkeeping work for farms and growers and keeps their savings for his gap. Pitches to Fenwick that the farm needs a data person and offers himself.
S2.feel: Anxious for Dev, and quietly hopeful for himself, which he doesn't tell Dev.
S2.quote: Then probably at midnight he'd want to make a spreadsheet of our money, because of course he would.
S2.fieldNote: The household risk sits with his partner, not him. He admits a hope he keeps from Dev, which is an honest gap between public and private. The pizza and kitchen-tidying story was warm and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains have to be shared, tax the share boom and pay people properly while they find new work. I'd join the protests, and I'd bring Dev. I'd be pretty loud about house prices too, because we rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the scary one for us right now. Dev's job is gone in this picture, not maybe, gone. My field job is safe, but it pays less than his, and I can't cover the rent on Station Road on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, we'd sit down and cut everything, the car goes, maybe. We'd look at a cheaper flat or moving in with his parents for a bit, which neither of us wants. I'd ask for every bit of overtime in the packhouse and push hard for the data role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's strange to feel safe and broke at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Dev work on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He could, actually. Fenwick needs people in the packhouse and someone to do the books properly. It'd be odd, working together, and he'd hate the cold. But I'd rather that than him sitting at home refreshing job sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people at the top who own the AI companies and the shares, and the government if it lets them keep it all. Not Dev's bosses, really, they'd be scared too. Not Fenwick either, he's just trying to get broccoli into boxes.

S3.say: I'd say tax the share boom and pay people properly while they find new work. I'd join the protests with Dev and be loud about house prices, since we rent.
S3.think: This is the scary one for us, because Dev's job is simply gone. My field job is safe but pays less, and I can't cover the rent alone.
S3.do: Cuts household spending in the first month, possibly selling the car, and looks at a cheaper flat or a stay with Dev's parents. Takes all packhouse overtime and suggests Dev work in Fenwick's packhouse or on the books.
S3.feel: Alarmed, feeling safe and broke at the same time.
S3.quote: It's strange to feel safe and broke at the same time.
S3.fieldNote: The most distressed he gets is when the office job at home goes, not his own. He's quick to find a fix, getting Dev into the packhouse, which shows his adaptable side. Safe and broke at once captures the whole household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be planned, with a fund for the crews and retraining paid for by the companies selling the robots. The pickers are mostly people from abroad on short visas, and they'd be dropped first with nothing. I'd say that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, and I feel bad saying it, I think this is the one where I could do well. Someone has to run the robots, fix the cutting arms, and plan their routes, and that's exactly the stuff I already do on the tablet. The crew is the one at real risk, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Fenwick and say, let me lead the robot trial. I'd ask the robot company for their training course and pay for it myself if I had to. And I'd help the crew, the translation, the forms for other jobs, whatever I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mixed up. Excited for the work, sick about the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Andrei, who's been coming every summer for nine years and taught me how to hold the knife. He sends money home to two kids. If a robot does broccoli, he doesn't get a visa next year, and that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you could do well. Is that a comfortable thought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's a bit like being picked for the team when your friends aren't. I'd take it, because we need the money, but I'd try to bring someone from the crew with me.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms must be planned, with a fund for crews and retraining paid for by the robot companies. The pickers on short visas would be dropped first with nothing.
S4.think: I feel bad saying it, but this is where I could do well, since running and fixing robots is close to my tablet work. The crew is really at risk, not me.
S4.do: Asks Fenwick to let him lead the robot trial and takes the robot company's training, paying himself if needed. Helps crew members with translation and forms for other jobs.
S4.feel: Mixed and anxious: excited about the work and sick about the crew.
S4.quote: If a robot does broccoli, he doesn't get a visa next year, and that's that.
S4.fieldNote: His mood falls from alarmed to anxious here because robots are his chance, which he admits with guilt. His worry turns to the visa crew, especially Andrei. He was the only one I've heard say the robots picture could be good for him personally.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one with no robots, the third, because that's the one that takes Dev's job and leaves us broke. What would help is pay while people retrain, real pay, for a year. And rent controls, honestly, because rent is what sinks us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pickers enough. People talk about farmers losing jobs, but on farms like ours it's the crews from abroad who'd go first, and they don't get a vote anywhere. Someone should interview Andrei.

headlineQuote: It's strange to feel safe and broke at the same time.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old field hand at a vegetable grower that supplies supermarkets, slow with the knife but the farm's go-to person for tablets and AI tools, which he uses daily. He blames supermarkets more than his boss and holds progressive views about pay, unions and the visa crews. His biggest risk is at home: his partner Dev is a junior accountant whose job disappears in the fast AI picture, leaving the couple short on rent. In the robot picture he sees a chance for himself, and feels guilty about the crew who'd lose out, especially an older picker named Andrei.
biggestWorry: The fast AI picture without robots, because Dev would lose his accounting job and they couldn't pay the rent on one field wage.
whatWouldHelp: Proper pay for a year while people retrain, and rent controls.
